analysis.one_liner: Phases out clearcutting and similar logging methods on national forests to protect soil, water, and wildlife.
analysis.headline: The bill to limit clearcutting in national forests drew 18 cosponsors but was referred to a House Agriculture subcommittee in May 1989 and died there without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten national forest planning rules to preserve each forest's natural mix of plant and animal life, and would have barred clearcutting, seed-tree, shelterwood, and other even-aged cutting on any national forest once 10 percent of its commercial timberland had been cut that way. It also let any citizen, state, or federal agency sue in court to enforce the limits, with legal fees available to winners. Timber contracts signed before enactment would have been untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or depends on national forests: hikers, campers, hunters, anglers, and downstream water users. The bill's stated purpose was to stop soil erosion, nutrient loss, loss of plant and animal diversity, and damage to recreation, wildlife, hunting, and fishing caused by intensive cutting [S3]. The citizen-suit provision would have given ordinary people and conservation groups a direct way to force compliance in court [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forest users, hunters, anglers, and downstream communities

how_it_helps.text: States the bill's purpose as protecting national forests from excessive clearcutting and the resulting soil erosion, nutrient losses, reduced diversity, impaired recreation, and harm to wildlife, hunting, and fishing [S3].

Once 10 percent of a national forest's commercial timberland has been cut by clearcutting, seed-tree, shelterwood, or large group-selection methods, all further use of those methods in that forest would be prohibited [S3].

Requires forest plans to preserve each stand's natural abundance of species, ecological communities, and genetic diversity, letting natural succession proceed as it would without human interference [S3].

Lets any person, state, or federal agency sue to enforce the cutting limits, with no advance notice required and attorney's fees available to the prevailing plaintiff — putting enforcement in citizens' hands rather than leaving it solely to the Forest Service [S3].
Grandfathers timber contracts already awarded, so loggers and mills with existing agreements would not have had them cancelled mid-deal [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and logging operations that harvest national forests, and the sawmills and mill towns that depend on that wood supply, would lose access to a large share of federal timber, since the even-aged methods the bill phases out are the cheapest way to log. The Forest Service's timber sale program, which shares receipts with counties, would also shrink. Some harvest would likely shift to private land or imports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber companies, sawmills, and logging towns

drawbacks.text: The 10-percent trigger is a hard cutoff, not a site-by-site judgment: even where a forester concluded clearcutting was the right tool for a particular stand or species, the bill would ban it outright once the threshold is reached, and it applies the same rule to forests with very different ecosystems [S3].

National forests are a major wood supply, and phasing out the cheapest harvesting methods would raise logging costs, cut mill jobs in timber-dependent towns, and push some harvest onto private land, where environmental rules are weaker, or onto imported wood [S3].

The no-notice citizen-suit provision with fee-shifting would make it easy to file lawsuits over cutting decisions, which supporters saw as enforcement but which courts and agencies would have had to absorb [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted real, documented harms from clearcutting — erosion, water damage, loss of wildlife habitat — and its grandfather clause softened the immediate hit to the industry. But the blunt 10-percent cutoff substituted a single number for professional judgment across very different forests, and the cost would fall heavily on timber-dependent communities, not just on large companies. A more graduated approach might have protected forests while easing the transition for mill towns. That trade-off was never debated on the floor, because the bill never got that far.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its forestry subcommittee, nothing further happened, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. John Bryant of Texas introduced the bill on May 18, 1989, with five original cosponsors from both parties [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture — the committee with jurisdiction over national forest logging [S5].
Five days later it was sent to the Subcommittee on Forests, Family Farms, and Energy, which is where most forestry bills go to be shaped or quietly shelved [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action is recorded for the rest of the 101st Congress, which ended January 3, 1991 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber companies, national forest timber purchasers, and the Forest Service's timber sale program came out ahead: clearcutting and other even-aged cutting on the national forests continued unchanged, and the public never got a hearing or a vote on the alternative.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Timber companies and national forest timber buyers

for.name: Rep. John W. Bryant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clearcutting Restraint Act of 1989 to phase out clearcutting and similar methods on national forests

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out; no hearing or markup is recorded in the action history

against.name: Subcommittee on Forests, Family Farms, and Energy
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 23, 1989 onward with no recorded action through the end of the Congress

against.name: Forest products industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed national forest clearcutting restrictions during this era, as it depended on federal timber sold largely through even-aged cutting

sides.party_line_note: Support was modest but bipartisan — 15 Democratic and 3 Republican cosponsors — and because the bill never reached a hearing or floor vote, no vote-based party split exists to measure.

industries.industry: Timber companies and national forest logging contractors
industries.note: The bill would have barred clearcutting and other even-aged methods on any national forest once 10 percent of its commercial timberland was cut that way, ending access to a major source of cheap federal timber. Its continuation under existing rules is the direct cost of the bill's protections for soil, water, and wildlife [S3].
Mills in timber-dependent regions relied on national forest logs; restricting harvest methods would shrink supply and raise costs, though the bill grandfathered contracts already awarded [S3].

The bill named impaired recreation and harm to wildlife, hunting, and fishing among the harms it targeted, so guides, outfitters, and tourism businesses in forest gateway towns stood to benefit from healthier forests [S3].
